parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is represented by a gravitational field line.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a gravitational field does - if you place a tiny test mass at a point, what vector quantity does the field exert on it?
Hint 2: Remember that for any field line, the tangent at a point gives a direction. Which direction of the force does this tangent show for that small mass?
parts.proper_answer: A gravitational field line shows the direction of the force acting on a (small test) mass placed in the field.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a field means**
Imagine placing a very small test mass $m$ at a point in space. The Earth pulls on it with a gravitational force $F = mg$. The field exists whether the test mass is there or not, but the test mass lets you feel it.

Step 2: **What the line adds**
The line through that point has its tangent along the force vector. So the line shows the direction of the force on the test mass at every point along it. Arrows point in the direction the mass would be pulled.

parts.label: (a)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: at least four radial lines from the Earth's surface, equally spaced around the surface

hints: Hint 1: Think about the shape of the Earth here - a uniform sphere. Towards which point must gravity always pull, and what does that imply for the shape of the lines outside?
Hint 2: Think about symmetry around a uniform sphere. How should the spacing of the lines compare on different sides, and which way should the arrows point?
parts.proper_answer: Draw at least four straight radial lines, equally spaced around the Earth, starting at the surface and pointing radially inward with arrows towards the centre of the Earth.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Radial because of a point-like pull**
Outside a uniform sphere, gravity acts as if all mass is at the centre. So every force points straight to the centre. That means field lines are straight radii, not curves.

Step 2: **Symmetric and inward**
Because the sphere is uniform, the pattern looks the same in all directions. Draw at least four lines equally spaced around the circle, e.g. up, down, left, right plus diagonals. Put arrows on each line pointing towards the Earth to show attraction.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 2.3, label the magnetic poles with the letters N and S to indicate which one is the magnetic N pole and which one is the magnetic S pole.

markscheme_points.text: top pole labelled S and bottom pole labelled N

hints: Hint 1: Recall the standard rule for the direction of magnetic field lines outside a magnet and compare it with the arrow directions already drawn entering the top and leaving the bottom in Fig. 2.3.
parts.proper_answer: Top magnetic pole is S, bottom magnetic pole is N. Field lines enter S and leave N outside.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the N to S rule**
Outside a magnet or solenoid, magnetic field lines always go from the N pole to the S pole. Inside they go from S to N to form closed loops.

Step 2: **Read the arrows**
In Fig. 2.3 the upper arrow points down into the Earth and the lower arrow points down away from the Earth. The line is leaving the bottom pole and entering the top pole. So the bottom must be the source $N$ and the top must be the sink $S$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: On Fig. 2.3, draw field lines to represent the Earth's magnetic field outside the Earth.

markscheme_points.text: solenoid field pattern at the poles: at least two field lines either side of both poles, close to the poles, clustered closely together, leaving the surface approximately perpendicularly to the surface and curving away from the axis of the poles as their distance from the surface increases

solenoid field pattern above the equator: at least one field line either side of the Earth connecting two points on the surface that are on the same side of the poles, one north of the equator and one south of it, passing above the surface near the magnetic equator approximately parallel to the surface

hints: Hint 1: Think about how field lines leave a pole of a bar magnet or solenoid - what angle do they make with the surface close to the pole and how do they spread as they go further out?

Hint 2: Think about how a line that starts on one side of the Earth can loop round and come back to the same side near the equator - what direction would it travel relative to the surface at the equator?
parts.proper_answer: Near each pole draw at least two lines each side leaving the surface almost perpendicularly, closely clustered and curving away from the axis with distance. Near the equator draw at least one line each side joining points north and south of the equator, passing above the surface approximately parallel to the surface.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pattern at the poles**
Close to a pole the field is strong and almost vertical. Draw lines that start perpendicular to the surface, packed closely together. As they get further from the surface they bend outward, away from the solenoid axis, to loop toward the opposite pole.

Step 2: **Pattern at the equator**
Field lines must form continuous loops from N to S outside. So a line leaving the southern hemisphere curves far out and re-enters the northern hemisphere on the same side of the Earth. Near the magnetic equator it skims above the surface, almost parallel to it. Draw at least one such loop on each side.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: An observer moves around the surface of the Earth.
parts.text: Use your answer in (a)(ii) to explain why the observed gravitational field of the Earth does not vary around the surface.

markscheme_points.text: (around the surface) lines are evenly spaced
all lines perpendicular to surface or pointing down towards surface (at all points around the surface)

hints: Hint 1: Look back at your radial pattern in (a)(ii) and focus on what an observer standing on the surface sees locally - how does the crowding of the lines at the surface compare from one place to another?
Hint 2: Think about the angle between the local lines and the ground. For a radial field from a sphere, what is that angle everywhere on the surface?
parts.proper_answer: Around the surface the field lines are evenly spaced, so field strength is the same everywhere. All lines are perpendicular to the surface / point vertically down, so direction relative to the surface is the same everywhere.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Same spacing means same strength**
Field line spacing shows field strength. Your (a)(ii) pattern has radial lines equally spaced around the circle. At the surface itself the separation is the same all round, so $g$ has the same magnitude for an observer anywhere on the surface.

Step 2: **Same angle means same direction**
Every radial line meets the spherical surface at $90^{\circ}$. So everywhere the field points straight down, perpendicular into the ground. There is no tilt that changes with position, so the observed field does not vary.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: With reference to your answer in (b)(ii), describe how the observed magnetic field of the Earth varies around the surface.

markscheme_points.text: Any three bulleted points from: strongest at the poles; weakest near the Equator; Up to two points from: perpendicular to surface at the poles; parallel to the surface near the Equator; angle to surface increases from Equator to poles

hints: Hint 1: Think about where your (b)(ii) lines are most crowded together and where they are most spread out - what does that tell you about where the field is strongest and weakest?
Hint 2: Think about standing at a magnetic pole versus at the magnetic equator - is the field line going into the ground or along the ground in each case?
Hint 3: Think about the journey between equator and pole - how does the tilt of the field to the surface change gradually?
parts.proper_answer: Magnetic field is strongest at the (magnetic) poles and weakest near the (magnetic) Equator. Field is perpendicular / vertical to the surface at the poles and parallel / horizontal to the surface near the Equator. The angle to the surface increases from Equator to poles.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Strength varies**
Line density shows strength. Near the poles in (b)(ii) the lines are clustered closely, so $B$ is largest there. Near the equator the loops are spread out high above the surface, so $B$ is smallest there.

Step 2: **Direction at the extremes**
At the poles the lines dive straight into or out of the ground, so the field is perpendicular to the surface, i.e. vertical. At the magnetic equator the lines skim parallel to the surface, i.e. horizontal.

Step 3: **Gradual change in between**
Moving from equator toward either pole, the field tilts more and more steeply into the ground. This tilt angle, often called dip or inclination, grows from about $0^{\circ}$ at the equator to $90^{\circ}$ at the poles, while the strength steadily increases.
